title: Caught “Pink-Handed”
caption: The star-forming region Gum 26, imaged by ESO's Very Large Telescope

recognition.text: ESO Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: A faint pinkish glow fills this view of Gum 26, a star-forming region found in Vela, the Sails, a constellation of the southern sky. It was imaged by the FORS instrument on ESO's Very Large Telescope in Chile.

Our galaxy contains many places like this, where new stars spring to life inside collapsing clumps of gas and dust. Gum 26 is an HII region, or emission nebula. Newly formed stars stream out intense ultraviolet radiation that ionizes the hydrogen gas around them, and that ionized gas gives off the pink glow.

Catching young stars pink-handed in this way is useful. By studying the glowing gas, astronomers can learn about the conditions in which stars form, and study how the newcomers then influence their surroundings.

understand.summary: The VLT's FORS2 instrument captured this visible-light image through B, V and R filters and a hydrogen-alpha filter. The color mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: A hydrogen filter and long exposures bring out a faint pink glow that the eye would struggle to see.

behind.exposure: Not published on the source page.
behind.technique: Not stated by the source (single frame, stack, mosaic or panorama unknown).

explore: The image was made through ESO's Cosmic Gems program, which uses telescope time unsuitable for science to create outreach images. Its data also go into ESO's science archive for astronomers.
alt: A cloud of gas glowing faintly pink among stars.
